summaries.example: Imagine a school where only boys may choose class leaders, even though girls and boys are equally able to help. Feminist philosophy would ask whether this rule is fair, what ideas support it, and how the school could change. It would also ask whether students with different backgrounds experience the rule in different ways.
summaries.summary: Feminist philosophy explores unfairness connected with gender and asks what a more just society could be like. Feminism is not only a political movement; it is also a group of ideas and questions. Feminist thinkers examine how social rules, traditions, language, and institutions shape people’s opportunities and identities. They also study how gender connects with race, class, ability, sexuality, nationality, and other parts of life. Different feminists use different approaches. Some focus on careful arguments, some on history and interpretation, and some on lived experience and practical change. Feminist philosophers have entered traditional fields such as ethics, political philosophy, science, religion, and the history of philosophy. They have also brought attention to subjects often treated as private or unimportant, such as care, family life, bodies, dependency, work, disability, and sexuality. Feminists do not agree on every question, including what equality means or how to define the group at the center of feminist work. The entry presents this variety as an important part of feminist inquiry rather than as a problem that must have one final answer.
key_ideas: Feminism is both a movement for social change and a way of thinking about justice.
Feminist philosophers study how rules, customs, language, and institutions can favor men or leave other people out.
They ask about topics that philosophy has sometimes ignored, including family life, care, bodies, work, disability, and reproduction.
There is no single feminist viewpoint. Feminists may disagree about identity, equality, freedom, and the best ways to create change.
Feminist philosophy uses many methods and connects with areas such as ethics, politics, science, history, and language.
summaries.why_it_matters: Feminist philosophy helps people notice unfair patterns that may seem normal. It shows that asking who is included, who is heard, and who benefits can improve our thinking about school, family, work, laws, knowledge, and everyday life. It also encourages careful attention to many different experiences when imagining social change.

important_terms.definition: A set of ideas and a movement that work to understand and end unfair treatment connected with gender.
Unfair treatment or harm that happens because people are placed into gender roles or judged by gender.
A way of looking at a question that notices details such as people’s bodies, lives, history, and social surroundings.
The practice of caring for people and the moral questions about who provides care and whose care is valued.
The belief that a rule or idea applies to everyone, even when it may come from one particular group’s experience.

questions_to_think_about: How can a rule seem fair but still make life harder for some people?
Whose experiences are missing when people say an idea applies to everyone?
Can people disagree about the best solution while still caring about justice?
What kinds of work or care are important but often not noticed?

summaries.example: Suppose a university says that its admissions rules are completely neutral because they use the same test for everyone. A feminist philosopher might ask whether the test reflects a narrow idea of achievement, whether students have had equal access to preparation, and whether social expectations influence who is encouraged to apply. Different approaches might analyze the language of the rule, its measurable effects, or the lived experiences of applicants. They may agree that the rule deserves scrutiny while disagreeing about the best remedy.
summaries.summary: The SEP presents feminist philosophy as both a political movement and an intellectual practice concerned with gender-related injustice. Its central work includes criticizing gender subordination, analyzing how it intersects with other forms of oppression, and considering possibilities for individual and collective resistance. Feminism cannot be reduced to a single demand for equal rights. Rights may be necessary, but oppression can also operate through social structures, culture, language, habits, and ideas about whose experiences count. Feminists therefore debate what justice requires and who or what should be the focus of feminist politics. The entry also warns that a simple historical “wave” model can hide differences within movements, continuities across periods, and contributions from women of color and working-class women. Feminist philosophy developed through several philosophical traditions. Analytic approaches often emphasize clarity and argument; continental approaches often emphasize interpretation, history, and critique; pragmatist approaches stress experience and inquiry; psychoanalytic approaches examine the formation of subjects and meanings. These distinctions matter, but the approaches also influence one another. Feminist philosophers have transformed traditional fields by challenging claims of neutrality and by studying topics such as care, dependency, labor, embodiment, disability, family, sexuality, reproduction, and knowledge. The result is not one unified theory, but an ongoing field shaped by disagreement, critique, and efforts toward social change.
key_ideas: Feminism combines diagnosis of gender subordination with efforts to imagine and produce social change.
Feminist inquiry questions supposedly neutral norms and examines how institutions, language, culture, and knowledge can exclude or marginalize people.
Feminist philosophers disagree about the meaning of equality, the category of woman, the relation between sex and gender, and which political or moral remedies are adequate.
The field includes analytic, continental, pragmatist, psychoanalytic, Latin American, and intersecting approaches; these are treated as different tools rather than simple opposing camps.
Feminist interventions reshape established fields, including ethics, epistemology, metaphysics, political philosophy, philosophy of science, law, religion, and aesthetics.
Attention to care, dependency, family, labor, disability, embodiment, sexuality, reproduction, and the self expands what counts as a philosophical subject.
summaries.why_it_matters: The field matters because philosophical theories can shape laws, institutions, research, and everyday judgments while presenting themselves as neutral. Feminist analysis tests those claims by asking whose standpoint produced them, who benefits, and who is excluded. It also broadens philosophical inquiry: personal and supposedly private experiences can reveal questions about justice, knowledge, freedom, identity, and power.

important_terms.definition: An intellectual commitment and political movement aimed broadly at understanding and ending oppression connected with gender.
A social order in which institutions, norms, and practices have historically favored men and supported men’s dominance.
The view that categories, identities, or meanings are shaped partly by social practices rather than being fixed only by nature.
A philosophical field that studies moral beliefs and practices while examining how gender and oppression shape them.
The capacity to make choices and act; feminist work often asks how social conditions support or restrict this capacity.
A claim that presents itself as applying to everyone, although it may reflect a particular social position or experience.
The idea that forms of oppression can interact, so gender cannot always be studied separately from race, class, ability, sexuality, or other identities.
A method or family of methods for investigating philosophical questions, such as analysis, interpretation, deconstruction, or attention to lived experience.

questions_to_think_about: What assumptions can hide inside a claim that a policy is neutral or universal?
Is equal legal treatment enough to end oppression, or must social and cultural structures also change?
How might different feminist methodologies produce different accounts of the same problem?
Can the category of woman be politically useful while remaining difficult to define universally?
How should feminist philosophy respond when gender interacts with race, class, disability, sexuality, or nationality?

summaries.example: A town council announces that every family should receive the same after-school schedule, calling the plan equal. Some students point out that families have different work hours, caring duties, transportation, and resources. A feminist philosopher might ask whether treating everyone identically really creates fair opportunities. Another philosopher might study how the word “family” is being used or whose experiences were considered when the plan was designed. They could disagree about the solution but still agree that the original rule needs closer examination.
summaries.summary: Feminist philosophy studies gender-related injustice and asks how people can build a more just society. The SEP describes feminism in two connected ways: as a political movement and as an intellectual project that develops concepts, arguments, and theories. Feminist thinkers investigate how gender norms can exclude or limit people, and how those norms connect with race, class, nationality, religion, ability, and sexuality. They do not all agree. Some emphasize equal rights, while others argue that rights alone cannot change unfair social structures, cultural expectations, language, or habits. There are also disagreements about how to define woman, how sex and gender relate, and which people should be central to feminist politics. The familiar idea that feminism has happened in a few historical “waves” can help organize events, but it can also hide differences within each period and ignore work outside mainstream politics. Feminist philosophy draws on several methods. Analytic philosophers often stress careful argument; continental philosophers often emphasize interpretation and historical critique; pragmatists focus on experience and practical inquiry; psychoanalytic approaches study how identity and social meanings develop. Feminists have also changed traditional philosophical subjects such as ethics, political philosophy, knowledge, science, law, religion, and aesthetics. In addition, they have asked philosophy to take seriously care, dependency, family, labor, bodies, disability, reproduction, sexuality, and other parts of life once treated as merely private.
key_ideas: Feminism is both a political movement and a philosophical inquiry into injustice, identity, power, and justice.
Feminist philosophers examine how laws, institutions, customs, language, and cultural expectations can make some people seem less important or capable.
Different feminists disagree about equality, the meaning of woman, the relationship between sex and gender, and the best forms of political change.
The history of feminism is more varied than a simple story of separate “waves,” because ideas and resistance continued across periods and included many groups.
Feminist philosophy uses several traditions and methods, including analytic, continental, pragmatist, and psychoanalytic approaches.
It has expanded philosophy’s subjects to include care, family, work, bodies, disability, sexuality, reproduction, science, and everyday experience.
summaries.why_it_matters: Feminist philosophy teaches us to look closely at ideas that seem ordinary or neutral. It asks who made a rule, whose experiences shaped it, who gains from it, and who may be left out. These questions can lead to better discussions about fairness in schools, families, workplaces, laws, science, and public life while recognizing that people’s experiences are not all the same.

important_terms.definition: A movement and set of ideas that challenge gender-related injustice and seek social change.
A pattern in which people are treated unfairly, excluded, or limited because of gender.
A system of social arrangements that has often placed men in positions of greater power than women.
A way of studying how different forms of disadvantage can overlap, such as gender, race, class, ability, or sexuality.
A person’s ability to make meaningful choices and act on them.
The belief that an idea or rule is true for everyone, even though it may reflect one group’s particular experience.
A general plan for asking and answering philosophical questions.
The study of moral ideas and practices, including how gender may shape judgments about right and wrong.

questions_to_think_about: When does treating everyone the same fail to produce fairness?
Why might a movement need a shared goal even when its members disagree about definitions?
How can language or cultural expectations limit people without an obvious law doing so?
What might be missed if a history of feminism focuses only on a few famous periods?
How could studying family life or care change ideas about justice?
